title: Forgotten Coding Queens, Telephones Untangled, and a Poisonous Quest: 8 Books We’re Excited to Read This November - Nautilus
gist: Nautilus deputy editor Bob Grant lists eight November books spanning Niels Bohr's physics, NSA women coders, the messy origins of the telephone, the curare quest that transformed surgical anesthesia, and political language. He frames the season as a chance to unplug from short-attention-span algorithms in favor of sustained reading.

insights.claim: Bob Grant argues that readers can choose to unplug from short-attention-span algorithms and use long-form books to sustain their focus.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Signals cultural pushback against algorithmic feeds, a modest headwind narrative for attention-driven platforms.
insights.quote: we can choose to unplug from the short-attention-span algorithms to dig into titles that engage our senses and sustain our focus
insights.locator: A chill is in the air

insights.claim: James Gleick's The Telephone: A New History argues the telephone's genesis was marked by intrigue, fraud and bribery rather than the tidy story of Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 invention.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: A reminder that foundational tech origins often involve contested IP and legal disputes.
insights.quote: But the genesis of the telephone was marked by intrigue, fraud, and bribery.

insights.claim: The telephone evolved from its messy origins to the present day, when people carry supercomputers masquerading as phones in their pockets.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Frames the smartphone as one of the most transformative inventions of the modern era.
insights.quote: each of us carries a supercomputer masquerading as a phone in our pockets

insights.claim: Eileen Buckholtz's Queens of Code tells the stories of 25 forgotten women technologists who worked in secret for decades at the National Security Agency.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Adds to a body of work challenging the idea that technology is a male field, relevant to tech workforce narratives.

insights.claim: Queens of Code joins Hidden Figures and Code Girls in a growing body of literature that dispels the myth that technology is a man's game.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Cultural narrative support for diversity in technology hiring.
insights.quote: dispels the myth that technology is a man’s game

insights.claim: Richard Gill's 1930s quest in the Ecuadorian Amazon for curare, a plant-derived poison, eventually produced a revolution in surgical anesthesia and a Nobel Prize.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Illustrates how bioprospecting of natural compounds has yielded major pharmaceutical breakthroughs.
insights.quote: The quest would eventually result in a revolution in surgical anesthesia and a Nobel Prize.

insights.claim: Gill sought to bring curare samples and preparation notes to pharmaceutical companies, which Matt O'Hara frames as an entanglement of scientific exploration and exploitation.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Highlights long-standing ethical tensions over pharma sourcing from Indigenous knowledge.

insights.claim: Philip Ball's book on Niels Bohr argues Bohr is overshadowed by Oppenheimer and Einstein despite building the model of the nucleus and seeding quantum mechanics.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Background on the roots of quantum mechanics; no direct market relevance.

insights.claim: Bob Grant frames the present as perilous times in which tyranny and greed threaten the freedoms philosophers helped codify over millennia.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Reflects elevated perceived political risk in cultural commentary.
insights.quote: Especially as we navigate these perilous times, when tyranny and greed threaten to undo the very freedoms philosophers have helped codify and secure over millennia.

insights.claim: Omekongo Dibinga argues that today's political rhetoric has become charged and dangerous, making America less inclusive, and that more thoughtful shared vocabulary offers a way out.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Points to political polarization as a persistent social backdrop.

insights.claim: Anthropologists Chris Knight and Jerome Lewis argue that female speech and expression steered human evolution away from violence toward more cohesive collectives, which in turn let language flourish.
insights.speaker: Bob Grant
insights.so_what: Academic theory of human origins; no direct investment relevance.
